Naming Ionic and Covalent Compounds: Ionic compounds are named cation first, then the anion with the ending -ide, and never use prefixes. A transition metal with several possible charges needs a Roman numeral, found from the charge needed to balance the anions, as in iron(III) oxide for Fe2O3. Polyatomic ions keep their names, such as nitrate, sulfate, hydroxide and ammonium. Covalent compounds of two nonmetals use the prefixes mono, di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa, hepta, octa, nona and deca, with no mono on the first element, so CO2 is carbon dioxide and N2O4 is dinitrogen tetroxide.
Writing Chemical Formulas: A chemical formula shows the elements in a compound and the ratio of their atoms or ions. For ionic compounds the total charge must be zero, and the criss-cross method turns the charge numbers into subscripts, which are then reduced to the lowest ratio. Polyatomic ions go in parentheses when more than one is needed, as in Ca(NO3)2, and the Roman numeral gives the metal charge. Covalent formulas come straight from the prefixes. A subscript multiplies the atom before it, and a subscript outside parentheses multiplies everything inside, so Ca3(PO4)2 has 13 atoms.
Chemical Equations and Balancing: A chemical equation shows reactants on the left, products on the right and state symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq). By the law of conservation of mass, atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so each element must have the same number of atoms on both sides. Equations are balanced only by changing coefficients, never subscripts, because changing a subscript changes the substance. Count atoms, adjust coefficients, leave hydrogen and oxygen for last, and reduce to the smallest whole numbers. Coefficients also give mole ratios, for example 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3.
Types of Chemical Reactions: Most reactions fit a few patterns. Synthesis combines substances into one product, A + B -> AB, and decomposition breaks one compound into simpler substances, AB -> A + B. In single replacement an element replaces another in a compound, A + BC -> AC + B. In double replacement two compounds exchange ions, AB + CD -> AD + CB, often forming a precipitate, a gas or water. A neutralization is a double replacement of an acid and a base. Combustion is a rapid reaction with oxygen, and complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water.
Predicting Products and Activity Series: To predict products, identify the reaction type, use correct ion charges to write the formulas and then balance. In the activity series a metal replaces another metal in a compound only if it is higher in the series, and metals above hydrogen replace hydrogen from acids, while Cu, Ag and Au do not. If the free element is lower, there is no reaction. A double replacement occurs only when a product is a precipitate, a gas or water, which is judged with solubility rules. If all products stay dissolved, such as with KNO3 and NaCl, there is no reaction.
